top_comments: Artificial analysis shows this: underperforming Qwen3.8 Flash Next and GLM 5.3 Flash, both of which you can run on a single B300 . I think Meta has a bit of catching up to do in the open-weight space.As an aside, it's really unfortunate that artificial analysis only provides comparison at the highest reasoning level, which is mostly unusable for high-volume production use cases. I would really like them to start providing comparisons at low and medium reasoning levels across these models because those tend to be the ones that actually get used in production.

Since there are many comments here arguing that this is not open weight, I looked at the license. Basically, you're free to use this except this clause:> If the Licensee or any of its affiliates provide a third party with access to artificial intelligence models as a product or service, via API or a similar interface, where the third party receives outputs of such models (“Model as a Service”), and the aggregate gross revenue of the Licensee and its affiliates exceeds twenty (20) million US dollars (or the equivalent in other currencies) during any consecutive twelve (12) month period, the Licensee must notify Meta and enter into a separate written agreement with Meta before offering the Software or any Derivatives as part of that Model as a Service business. This Section 3 does not apply to (a) internal use, research, or any commercial activity that is not Model as a Service, or (b) the Licensee's use of the Software as a component to power features of the Licensee's own product or service that is not a Model as a Service.They're allowing the use of this in commercial products, just not selling the model directly.

Like I said last week. I think zucks original llama thesis is proving more correct by the week. The rent market on intelligence never materialized, if you have THE frontier model, you can charge rent (for a few weeks, maybe month). But after a certain capability level it's price that drives the decision.Zuck is doing the thing he's really good at, and building a moat around the network (Muse is VERY sticky), and now that we're all going to standardize on Meta's model, we're going to optimize the heck out of the infra to run the model making it cheaper for him to scale, thus bringing in more participants to his network, and thus making his network more valuable.Meta is going to win consumer AI.

Nick is a force of nature. Highly recommend following him on X if you don't already.His launch post gives good context not found in the blog:> interpretability might be the most important scientific problem in the world right now, as I don't think we can solve alignment if we don't know what we're building. I think I have good news about it. I co-authored early work in mechanistic interpretability at OpenAI and came away pessimistic, because neural networks appeared to fold into arbitrary tangled knots. years later, I started openai's first large-scale automated interpretability project, finding about 2% of neurons legible with the primitive tools we had> with modern agentic tools and a much closer look, the picture looks totally different. the vast majority in models up to trillions of parameters are legible, and their circuits beautiful. many famous examples of tangled neurons turned out to be misunderstood. The roadblocks I expected mostly aren't there. I now think ambitious interpretability will be solved by the time we need it most, and possibly quite soon, as automated scientists keep improving. it may be a bitter lesson for interpretability: the simple thing, at absurd scale, workshttps://x.com/nickcammarata/status/2110757819427574056?s=46

The claims seem to be an overreach of what is actually proven. We've known about progressive feature complexity and the impacts of early training structures on later training for a really long time (since CNN's, The Lottery Ticket Hypothesis, etc...) and neither of those phenomenon are mutually exclusive with parameter overloading. The Multimodal Gap work (https://arxiv.org/abs/2203.02053) seems to imply networks have a tendency towards condensed representations that are clearly not semantic and a bunch of other considerations are already on the table for discussion. I don't think these have all been considered sufficiently to start claiming we are around the corner from mechanistic interpretation.

I'm confused - it seems to be saying that, instead of thinking about neurons as packing together a lot of "concepts" together into one, the issue is that your view of what a "concept" is, was already prejudiced, and the neuron itself had a small clean role? Like, you can either think about this as the "Cat & Car" neuron or you can think about it as the "V shaped neuron" - one seems simpler.But isn't the point that the neural nets learn some insanely abstract ideas anyways? So whether the complexity is "ahh we think this neuron does 100 seemingly unrelated things but we don't understand it" or "this actually is some kind of latent shared feature, but we don't know what the concept represents because the composition of the entire circuit is an arcane algorithm", we're kind of stuck, no?This seems like a classic model-description issue more than anything.

Modern machinery feels so insubstantial, emphasizing clean glass and tidy machined chassis. (chassies?)I have this persistent daydream about a computer setup that feels like the Nostromo flight deck from Alien. I almost want to feel like I'm sitting _inside_ a computer when I'm at my desk, surrounded by powerful feeling electronics with substantial switches and such. Of course there's plenty of inconvenience there too, but something about it appeals to me.

I want more stuff like this. The era 20 years ago (e.g. Enlightenment) was way more fun than the bland monotonic design we have these days. If you like bland modern design, great, that should be an option as well, but we should still have good variety.

One of my greatest AI-related fears is that we build critical systems into kafkaesque hellscapes.Yes, nukes would be bad to give control to an AI with no workaround. But so are customer service groups of fraud departments at banks. A kafkaesque hellscape is where a customer or beneficiary of your service cannot get the help they need by policy and by design. Like getting Google on the phone, getting a non-scripted human 10 years ago in a call center, or now getting a non-agentic interaction on the phone. The scripts dominate the interaction.The IRS, for a time, would cut off your call if their wait system was too busy. articles.title: Krea 3 – An image model built for editing at scale
articles.summary: Krea 3 – An image model built for editing at scale

top_comments: Hello HN,This is Diego from Krea. Today we are announcing the open beta of Krea 3, our newest foundational image model.In a nutshell, it’s a frontier image model in terms of quality, but at a fraction of the speed and a fraction of the price.We will be releasing a more technical update, like we did with Krea 2 (https://www.krea.ai/blog/krea-2-technical-report), but this website shows the capabilities we focused on:* Native regional edits* Precise edits so that there is minimal area degradation pixel-wise* Frontier image quality. Benchmarks still being worked on, but in our internal evals it seems a no-brainer replacement to NBP or GPT Image, both speed and cost-wise.* Faster edits (AFAICK, this should unlock a pareto frontier for speed in frontier edit models).In terms of future updates, the team is thinking about letting folks fine-tune Krea 3 (via LoRAs) and open-weights, but we’re still in the middle of launch hiccups and then we’ll revisit the next iterations.Thanks!

Comparison samples with GPT-Image-2.5 for UI design work:Starship landing pageKrea 3: https://image.non.io/80b85aaa-286b-4ad7-b3ae-cfab4b491216.we...GPT-Image-2.5: https://image.non.io/19c5f032-cbc7-4034-9682-3aba451bd669.we...Fashion history websiteKrea 3: https://image.non.io/a6e61219-963c-4921-b453-738960e03308.we...GPT-Image-2.5: https://image.non.io/c067fd76-9c7e-46c2-a8fd-0b0931bf93f6.we...Banking websiteKrea 3: https://image.non.io/3a1e7b50-36e7-418c-ab47-368ce4f01948.we...GPT-Image-2.5: https://image.non.io/b96a7e00-3289-4044-90de-e0f86a2ca55e.we...Overall Krea 3 isn't near GPT-Image-2.5 in terms of visual creativity in this space, but it still should be commended for its ability to render small text details. That said despite it specifying you can add exact hex codes as color reference, I've found that they tend to leak into the design (check the valuation panel of the banking website - notice to the right of the "fixed indexed 7-yr" there's a hex code that made it into the image).I'd love to get my hands on this to post-train and see if it can be pushed further in this space. I actually see a lot of potential for the model, despite the clear differences in the examples above.

articles.title: Someone on Torrent Sites Kept Fucking with My Sonarr
articles.summary: Someone on Torrent Sites Kept Fucking with My Sonarr

top_comments: Sonarr has an advanced setting in "Settings > Indexers > [Your indexer] > Fail Downloads" which you should add "Executables" to. Then these kinds of downloads get automatically marked as failed/blacklisted and a new search and new download is attempted without you needing to manually intervene. You may also have to tweak some conflicting settings on qbit.Alternatively, if there's a way to have qbit itself mark the download as "Failed" when it detects and refuses to download an executable, that would work too. I don't use qbit personally so I don't know if that's a thing it can be configured to do.
